chain.label: Parallel runway 28L closed overnight for construction
chain.trigger: SFO parallel runway 28L was scheduled to be closed at 2300

chain.label: Air Canada's ineffective presentation of NOTAM and approach-chart information
chain.trigger: the presentation of that information did not effectively convey the importance of the runway closure information and promote flight crew review and retention

chain.label: Night visual approach with runway 28L dark and construction lights on the field
chain.trigger: Night visual meteorological conditions prevailed at the time of the incident; SFO lighting logs indicated that the lights on runway 28L were turned off about 2312

chain.label: Four air carrier airplanes queued on taxiway C awaiting departure
chain.trigger: Four air carrier airplanes... were on taxiway C awaiting clearance to take off from runway 28R

caused_by.evidence: Because of the runway 28L closure on the night of the incident, airplanes were using taxiway C to depart from runway 28R

chain.label: Both pilots fatigued from continued wakefulness and circadian disruption
chain.trigger: the captain had been awake for more than 19 hours, and the first officer had been awake for more than 12 hours. Thus, the captain and the first officer were fatigued during the incident flight

chain.label: No taxiway-landing alerting available in cockpit or tower (no SmartLanding/RAAS; ASSC cannot detect taxiway arrivals)
chain.trigger: the ASSC system was not designed to predict an imminent collision involving an arriving airplane lined up with a taxiway; thus, the ASSC system did not produce an alarm

chain.label: Crew's ineffective review of the runway 28L closure NOTAM in the flight release and ATIS; closure never briefed as a threat
chain.trigger: both pilots' failure to assimilate the runway 28L closure information included in the ATIS information

caused_by.evidence: this level of emphasis was not effective in prompting the flight crewmembers to review and/or retain this information, especially given the NOTAM's location
human limitations (such as fatigue and time pressure/workload) may affect the review of information

chain.label: First officer omitted the required manual ILS tuning and captain did not verify it, leaving no backup lateral guidance
chain.trigger: the first officer did not comply with Air Canada's procedures to tune the ILS frequency... and the captain did not comply with company procedures to verify the ILS frequency

caused_by.evidence: the instruction on the approach chart to manually tune the ILS frequency was not conspicuous during the crew's review of the chart
Possible explanations for the breakdowns in CRM during the incident flight include fatigue

chain.label: Expectation bias: crew expected two open parallel runways and identified lighted taxiway C as runway 28R
chain.trigger: the cues available to the flight crewmembers to indicate that the airplane was aligned with a taxiway were not sufficient to overcome their belief, as a result of expectation bias, that the taxiway was the intended landing runway

caused_by.evidence: the flight crewmembers' lack of awareness about the runway 28L closure... led to their expectation to identify two runway surfaces during the approach and resulted in their incorrect identification of taxiway C instead of runway 28R
he thought that he saw runway lights for runway 28L and believed that runway 28R was runway 28L and that taxiway C was runway 28R
particularly in night VMC when fewer cues were available to pilots to aid in airport and runway identification
fatigue... could lead to higher susceptibility for expectation bias and increased difficulty of overcoming expectation bias once it occurs

chain.label: Captain's late request for the first officer to set runway heading prolonged his heads-down time at the final waypoint
chain.trigger: the captain's request, at the final waypoint (F101D), for the first officer to set the runway heading, which took the first officer by surprise and prolonged his heads-down time while the airplane was aligned with the taxiway

caused_by.evidence: Possible explanations for the breakdowns in CRM during the incident flight include fatigue... and the high workload associated with the approach

chain.label: Captain made the 14-degree turn at F101D onto taxiway C instead of runway 28R
chain.trigger: the captain made the required 14 degree right turn to align the airplane with runway 28R but instead aligned the airplane with taxiway C

caused_by.evidence: the flight crew's misidentification of taxiway C as the intended landing runway
the crewmembers could not take advantage of the ILS's lateral guidance capability to help ensure proper surface alignment

the first officer's focus on tasks inside the cockpit after the airplane passed the final waypoint reduced his opportunity to effectively monitor the approach and recognize that the airplane was not aligned with the intended landing runway

chain.label: Approach continued over occupied taxiway C to 100 ft over UAL1 and 60 ft over PAL115
chain.trigger: ACA759 overflew UAL1 at an altitude of 100 ft... reaching a minimum altitude of about 60 ft at 2356:07 as the airplane overflew PAL115

caused_by.evidence: the flight crew aligned the airplane with parallel taxiway C instead
only 10 to 20 ft of vertical separation between the ACA759 and PAL115 airplanes
such technology, if it had been installed on the incident airplane, could have helped the flight crew identify its surface misalignment error earlier in the landing sequence

chain.label: Low-altitude go-around initiated at 89 ft prevented collision; uneventful second approach and landing
chain.trigger: The flight crew-initiated, low-altitude go-around over the taxiway prevented a collision between the Air Canada airplane and one or more airplanes on the taxiway

caused_by.evidence: multiple salient cues of the surface misalignment were present as the airplane approached the airport seawall, and one or more of these cues likely triggered the captain's initiation of a go-around
